Eggs of the black grouper, measuring 0.95 millimeters in diameter, yield larvae with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams]. This minuscule initial mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy common among epinephelids, where females release large quantities of small, buoyant eggs into the water column. Incubation proceeds rapidly at a water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], with yolk-sac larva emergence occurring after only 7 days [ab = 7 days]. The resulting prolarvae are entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves for their first few days of life before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. This brief endotrophic interval is typical for warm-water serranids, where elevated temperatures accelerate chorionase activity and yolk absorption rates. The tiny hatchlings, still bearing a conspicuous yolk sac, must quickly locate suitable planktonic prey to avoid the point of no return associated with complete yolk depletion. Field observations suggest that the first exogenous feeding event occurs within 24 to 48 hours of eclosion, a critical window that strongly influences early larval survival and subsequent recruitment into juvenile nursery habitats.

As juvenile black grouper grow and approach the transition to benthic life, their body length increases steadily until they attain the total length at puberty of 67.7 centimeters [Lp = 67.7 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty is estimated at 4,000 grams [Wwp = 4,000 grams], calculated from the length–weight relationship established for Mycteroperca bonaci in the Gulf of Mexico. This relationship, based on extensive field sampling, indicates that animals must surpass a substantial size threshold before the HPG axis activates and gametogenesis begins. The onset of gonadal recrudescence marks a pivotal life-history shift, as individuals reallocate resources from somatic growth toward reproductive investment. At a controlled water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], field-caught specimens exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 4% [GSI = 4%]. This reproductive pattern, common among iteroparous serranids, allows females to spread reproductive effort across several months and buffer against interannual variability in prey availability.

Fully mature adults of this species can achieve a maximum recorded total length of 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 45,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 45,400 grams]. This substantial body size places Mycteroperca bonaci among the larger members of its genus, capable of dominating reef habitats and occupying an apex predatory role within its ecosystem. The length–weight relationship used to derive this asymptotic mass was validated against a large dataset of landed individuals collected from commercial and recreational fisheries throughout the Caribbean. Such large-bodied individuals are typically decades old, as growth in epinephelids is relatively slow after sexual maturity. The extended longevity of this species is underscored by a maximum lifespan of 91 years [am = 91 years] at an ambient temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], making it one of the longest-lived teleosts known from tropical marine environments. This remarkable lifespan is comparable to that of certain deep-water rockfishes and suggests a conservative life-history strategy characterized by delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output over many decades.

The protracted lifespan of the black grouper is closely tied to its slow maturation schedule and the substantial time required to achieve the size necessary for successful spawning. Compared to other epinephelids, the black grouper's total length at puberty of 67.7 centimeters [Lp = 67.7 centimeters] and corresponding wet weight at puberty of 4,000 grams [Wwp = 4,000 grams] indicate a particularly slow route to sexual maturation, which is consistent with its extreme longevity and late age at first reproduction. This delayed reproductive onset is a hallmark of long-lived, late-maturing predators and makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as removal of large, fecund individuals can rapidly deplete the reproductive potential of a local population. At the spawning aggregation sites, the gonadosomatic index of 4% [GSI = 4%] was measured at 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. Fishery managers often use this index to determine whether the aggregation is in an early, peak, or late phase of spawning activity, thereby helping to set appropriate seasonal closures.

Comparative studies with other serranids reveal that the life-history parameters of Mycteroperca bonaci align closely with those of congeneric species from similar thermal regimes. The maximum total length of 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters] and the corresponding ultimate wet weight of 45,400 grams [Wwi = 45,400 grams] are consistent with values reported for the Warsaw grouper and the Goliath grouper, though the asymptotic size of the black grouper is somewhat smaller than either of those relatives. At 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], the age at birth of 7 days [ab = 7 days] is comparable to the incubation period observed in the coney Cephalopholis fulva, despite considerable differences in adult body size. The maximum lifespan of 91 years [am = 91 years] at an ambient temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C] is notably longer than that of most tropical groupers, which rarely exceed 40 to 50 years in the wild, and may reflect a combination of genetic predisposition and the relatively stable, cool thermal environment inhabited by older, deeper-dwelling individuals. These comparative data underscore the importance of considering species-specific thermal physiology when modeling the demographic responses of groupers to climate change.
